full_title: ANONYMOUS, COMPLAINANT, VS. HON. JULIETO N. BAJAN, PRESIDING JUDGE, BRANCH 2, MUNICIPAL TRIAL COURT IN CITIES, SURIGAO CITY, SURIGAO DEL NORTE, RESPONDENT.
docket: A.M. No. MTJ-25-035 [Formerly JIB FPI No. 21-053-MTJ]
subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
syllabus_topic: IX. Legal and Judicial Ethics > B. Judicial Ethics (CJCA) > 2. Accountability of Members of the Judiciary > a. Judicial Accountability and Disciplinary Proceedings (Canon VII)
topics: Retirement does not oust the Court of administrative jurisdiction
Habitual tardiness, smoking in court, hearing other courts' cases, sleeping during trial (Revised Rule 140)
Ignoring OCA and JIB directives to comment is gross insubordination
Rule 140, Section 4 does not automatically make a judge's offense a ground for discipline as a lawyer
Penalties for multiple offenses; second offense; fine in lieu of suspension for a retired judge

other_subjects.subject: Political and Public International Law
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VI. Judicial Department > E. The Supreme Court > 1. Composition, Powers, and Functions > b. Administrative Supervision over Lower Courts

doctrine:
Once administrative jurisdiction attaches (the complaint was filed while the respondent was in office), the judge's later **retirement does not oust the Court of jurisdiction or make the case moot** (reiterated, OCA v. Fuensalida). Under Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC): smoking in court and in chambers against the Court's anti-smoking issuances, and hearing cases of other courts without authority against OCA Circular No. 90-2004 (only the Supreme Court may change the venue or place of trial, Const., Art. VIII, Sec. 5(4)), are each a **violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars** (less serious, Sec. 15(e)). Starting sessions at 11:00 to 11:30 a.m. is **habitual tardiness** (less serious, Sec. 15(c)); "a judge's work is 24/7" is no excuse. Sleeping during trial is **simple misconduct** violating Canon 4, Section 1 (propriety) of the New Code of Judicial Conduct (Sec. 15(a)). **Repeatedly ignoring OCA and JIB directives to comment is gross insubordination**, a serious charge. Only gross insubordination, not simple insubordination, is an offense under Revised Rule 140.

The Court **clarified** that Section 4 of Revised Rule 140 **does not automatically make a judge liable as a lawyer** for every improper act that has a matching provision in the CPRA or the Lawyer's Oath. The Court must first ask whether the misconduct casts serious doubt on the judge's moral fitness and integrity as a member of the Bar. Added sanctions as a lawyer are confined to patently unlawful acts, immorality, abuse of power, and deceitful or dishonest conduct, among others, that clearly reflect on personal character. Acts that pertain to the performance of official functions (tardiness, smoking, hearing cases outside the proper court, sleeping in trial) do not qualify.

On penalties: a separate penalty is imposed for each offense (Sec. 21). A retired judge who can no longer be suspended is fined. Length of service is not mitigating if the judge has a prior disciplinary record. A repeat offense after a warning may justify a fine up to double the maximum (Sec. 20). The Court may, in its discretion, decline to order forfeiture of retirement benefits even for a serious charge.
facts:
Two undated anonymous letter-complaints from litigants, who hid their identities for fear of reprisal, were sent to the Office of the Chief Justice and to the Executive Judge of the MTCC of Surigao City. They accused Judge Julieto N. Bajan, Presiding Judge of Branch 2, MTCC Surigao City, of starting trial at 11:30 a.m. instead of 8:30 a.m. and keeping parties waiting more than two hours only to postpone, of smoking and sleeping during trial, and of hearing in Surigao City cases raffled to another court (MTCC Placer-Bacuag). Judge Bajan also held designations as acting presiding judge of other stations.

The OCA referred the complaints to the RTC and MTCC Executive Judges of Surigao City for discreet investigation. Both confirmed that Judge Bajan held hearings only from about 11:00 or 11:30 a.m. to 1:00 p.m., smoked in open court until November 2012 and still smoked in chambers, did not report daily to his regular court, and slept during trial so that lawyers had to leave. They also confirmed that he heard at MTCC Branch 2 one case from Placer-Bacuag and one from Sison-Tagana-an. No apparent or serious delay in acting on cases was found.

In a letter-comment dated February 28, 2014, Judge Bajan asked for dismissal of the second complaint as harassment. He attacked its lack of verification and supporting records, not its substance. The OCA's May 2, 2014 directive to file a more comprehensive comment went unheeded despite a tracer (July 24, 2015) and a reiteration (February 1, 2021). The OCA referred the matter to the JIB, whose Office of the General Counsel filed a formal complaint. The JIB twice directed him to file a verified comment (May 10, 2022 and March 9, 2023). The second directive also required him to show cause why he should not be disciplined as a member of the Bar and warned that non-compliance would be a waiver. He did not comply. He retired on May 23, 2023.

The JIB recommended that the matter be re-docketed and that he be fined PHP 50,000.00 for each of six offenses. These were habitual absenteeism or tardiness, smoking, sleeping during hearings (simple misconduct), hearing cases not raffled to him, simple neglect of duty for delay, and simple misconduct as a member of the Bar.
issues: Whether the Court retains jurisdiction over the administrative case despite Judge Bajan's retirement.
Whether Judge Bajan is liable for violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars for smoking within court premises and for hearing cases of other courts.
Whether he is liable for habitual tardiness, and for simple neglect of duty for delay in resolving cases.
Whether sleeping during trial is simple misconduct constituting a violation of the New Code of Judicial Conduct.
Whether his failure to comply with the OCA's and the JIB's directives to comment is gross insubordination.
Whether he should also be disciplined as a member of the Philippine Bar for the same acts.
ruling:
**1. Yes, the Court retains jurisdiction.** Jurisdiction attaches when the complaint is filed during the respondent's incumbency and is "not lost by the mere fact that the public official or employee was no longer in office during the pendency of the case." Retirement is not a ground to dismiss the case or render it moot (OCA v. Fuensalida).

**2. Yes, two counts of violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars (less serious, Sec. 15(e), Revised Rule 140).** (a) *Smoking:* Memorandum Circular No. 01-2008 and Office Order No. 06-2009 prohibit smoking inside court buildings and adjacent areas; smoking is allowed only in designated places. Judge Bajan smoked openly during trial and in chambers, despite complaints from court staff. (b) *Hearing other courts' cases:* Under the Constitution only the Supreme Court can order a change of venue or place of trial. OCA Circular No. 90-2004 requires that cases remain in the branch to which they were raffled. By hearing and bringing cases of other courts to his sala, he inconvenienced litigants, jeopardized the safekeeping of records and evidence, and "arrogated upon himself authority no less than only the High Court possesses."

**3. Liable for habitual tardiness (less serious, Sec. 15(c)), but not for simple neglect of duty.** OCA Circular No. 63-2001 (then in force) and OCA Circular No. 250-15 require session hours of 8:30 a.m. to 12 noon and 2:00 to 4:30 p.m. He began sessions between 11:00 and 11:30 a.m. while the public arrived as early as 8:30 a.m. His excuse that a judge's mental work is "24/7" was unacceptable. Circulars on session hours "are not just empty pronouncements." However, neither investigating judge confirmed any delay in his cases, so there was no factual basis for the JIB's recommended finding of simple neglect of duty.

**4. Yes, simple misconduct (Sec. 15(a)).** Misconduct is an intentional wrongdoing or deliberate violation of a rule or standard of behavior connected with official functions. Gross misconduct requires corruption, clear intent to violate the law, or flagrant disregard of established rules. Scandalous behavior that erodes public esteem for the Judiciary is simple misconduct. Falling asleep during trial, so that lawyers had to step out, violated Canon 4, Section 1 of the New Code of Judicial Conduct, which requires judges to avoid impropriety and its appearance.

**5. Yes, gross insubordination, a serious charge.** Directives of the OCA, issued in the exercise of the Court's administrative supervision, and of the JIB, to which the Court delegated the processing of complaints, "are not mere requests" and must be obeyed promptly and completely. Insubordination is the "inexplicable and unjustified refusal to obey some order that a superior is entitled to give and have obeyed." Unlike the 2017 RACCS, Revised Rule 140 retains only gross insubordination as an offense. For more than 10 years Judge Bajan ignored the OCA's directive to file a comprehensive comment and the JIB's two directives to file a verified comment. Compliance cannot be partial or selective (Judge Santiago v. Fernando; Beltran v. Pabica). His indifference showed defiance of the Court itself.

**6. No, he is not separately disciplined as a lawyer.** The OGC complaint did not seek his liability as a lawyer, though the JIB recommended it under the CPRA. **Section 4 of Revised Rule 140 "does not contemplate automatically holding judges liable for all improper acts that have a corresponding provision under the CPRA or the Revised Lawyer's Oath."** The CPRA and the Oath are broad, so nearly every act of a judge could otherwise be a ground for discipline as a lawyer. The Court must assess whether the judge's transgressions "cast serious doubt on his or her moral fitness." Added discipline is confined to patently unlawful acts, immorality, abuse of power, and deceitful or dishonest conduct, among others, that clearly reflect on personal character or fitness to practice law. Smoking in court, ignoring session hours, hearing cases outside the proper court, and sleeping during trial pertain to his official functions. They do not rise to a level of moral delinquency warranting bar discipline.

**7. Penalties.** Separate penalties are imposed for each offense (Sec. 21). Being retired, he can no longer be suspended, so fines are imposed. His more than 10 years of service is not mitigating because he had prior administrative liabilities: A.M. No. MTJ-20-1941 (including PHP 20,000.00 for habitual tardiness, with a stern warning), A.M. No. MTJ-16-1868, and A.M. No. P-17-3707. The Court fined him PHP 50,000.00 each for the two circular violations and for simple misconduct. Habitual tardiness drew PHP 100,000.00, the maximum for a less serious charge, as his second offense after a warning. Gross insubordination drew **PHP 300,000.00, above the PHP 200,000.00 ceiling for serious charges**, because it was a second offense and to stress strict compliance with directives to comment. The Court chose not to forfeit his retirement benefits out of compassion, though not as a mitigating circumstance. It considered his multiple designations (Executive Judge and acting judge of two other stations), that gross insubordination was his only serious charge, and the absence of evidence that he neglected his judicial duties.
disposition: Retired Judge Julieto N. Bajan was found GUILTY under A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC of: (1) two counts of violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars (Sec. 15(e)) for smoking during trial and within court premises and for hearing cases from other courts, fined PHP 50,000.00 each; (2) habitual tardiness (Sec. 15(c) in relation to Sec. 20), fined PHP 100,000.00; (3) simple misconduct constituting a violation of the New Code of Judicial Conduct (Sec. 15(a)), fined PHP 50,000.00; and (4) gross insubordination, fined PHP 300,000.00. The aggregate fine of PHP 550,000.00 is payable within 30 days from finality; if unpaid, contempt proceedings under Rule 71, Section 3 shall be commenced. Copies were furnished to the Office of the Bar Confidant, the IBP, and the OCA.

bar_questions.q: Judge Cruz of a Municipal Trial Court in Cities was the subject of an anonymous complaint. The OCA directed him to comment. He sent a one-page letter calling the complaint harassment and pointing out that it was unverified, without addressing the charges. The OCA twice directed him to submit a comprehensive comment, and the Judicial Integrity Board later twice directed him to file a verified comment. He ignored all four directives. While the case was pending, Judge Cruz compulsorily retired. (a) Should the case be dismissed because of his retirement? (b) What is his administrative liability for ignoring the directives?

alac.answer: (a) No. The Court retains jurisdiction despite his retirement. (b) He is liable for gross insubordination, a serious charge under Revised Rule 140.
alac.legal_basis: Once jurisdiction attaches because the complaint was filed during the respondent's incumbency, it is not lost by his later retirement, which neither warrants dismissal nor renders the case moot (OCA v. Fuensalida, as applied in Anonymous v. Judge Bajan, A.M. No. MTJ-25-035, March 4, 2025). Directives of the OCA and the JIB to comment are issued in the exercise of the Court's administrative supervision over lower courts and are not mere requests. Under Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC), which retains only gross insubordination as an offense, a judge's repeated and unjustified failure to comply with them is gross insubordination, a serious charge (Anonymous v. Judge Bajan, supra).
alac.application: (a) The complaint was filed and acted upon while Judge Cruz was still in office, so the Court's jurisdiction had attached; his compulsory retirement does not end the case. (b) His one-page letter dodged the substance of the charges, and compliance with a directive to comment cannot be partial or selective. He then ignored two OCA directives and two JIB directives without explanation. That is a willful disregard of lawful orders from offices acting for the Supreme Court. Because he can no longer be suspended or dismissed, the Court may impose a fine or, in lieu of dismissal, forfeiture of benefits (except accrued leave credits) under Revised Rule 140.
alac.conclusion: The case proceeds despite retirement, and Judge Cruz is liable for gross insubordination.

bar_questions.q: In an administrative case against Judge Reyes, the Judicial Integrity Board found him guilty of habitual tardiness, smoking inside his courtroom, and sleeping during trial. After requiring him to show cause, the JIB also recommended that he be fined as a member of the Bar for violating Canon II (Propriety) of the Code of Professional Responsibility and Accountability, relying on Section 4 of Rule 140, as amended. Should the Supreme Court also discipline Judge Reyes as a lawyer?

alac.answer: No. The Court should not impose an additional sanction on Judge Reyes as a member of the Bar for these acts.
alac.legal_basis: Section 4 of Rule 140, as amended by A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC, allows an administrative case against a judge to be considered a disciplinary case against him as a lawyer. However, it does not automatically hold judges liable as lawyers for every improper act that has a counterpart in the CPRA or the Lawyer's Oath. The Court first determines whether the misconduct casts serious doubt on the judge's moral fitness as a member of the Bar. Additional sanctions are confined to patently unlawful acts, immorality, abuse of power, and deceitful or dishonest conduct, among others, that clearly reflect on personal character (Anonymous v. Judge Bajan, A.M. No. MTJ-25-035, March 4, 2025).
alac.application: Habitual tardiness, smoking in court, and sleeping during trial are improper and are punishable under Rule 140 as offenses of a judge. But they pertain to the performance of his official functions. They do not involve dishonesty, deceit, immorality, or abuse of power that would put in question his fitness to remain a lawyer. That the JIB issued a show-cause order satisfies due process, but it does not by itself justify a second sanction. The result could differ if the acts showed moral delinquency, such as dishonest or deceitful conduct.
alac.conclusion: Judge Reyes should be penalized only as a judge, not additionally as a member of the Bar.

bar_questions.q: Judge Lim presides over an MCTC in Municipality A and was designated acting presiding judge of an MTCC in City B, 40 kilometers away. To save travel time, he ordered several cases pending in the MCTC of Municipality A, which were still at the trial stage, brought to City B and heard there, without authority from the Supreme Court. (a) Did Judge Lim act within his authority? (b) What administrative offense, if any, did he commit?

alac.answer: (a) No. Only the Supreme Court may order a change of venue or place of trial. (b) He committed a violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars, a less serious charge under Revised Rule 140.
alac.legal_basis: Article VIII, Section 5(4) of the Constitution vests in the Supreme Court the power to order a change of venue or place of trial to avoid a miscarriage of justice. Section 6 gives it administrative supervision over all courts. To implement these, OCA Circular No. 90-2004 provides that, except as stated in the guidelines, all cases shall remain in the branch to which they were raffled or assigned. A judge who hears and transfers cases of other courts to his station without authority commits a violation of Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars under Section 15(e) of Revised Rule 140 (Anonymous v. Judge Bajan, A.M. No. MTJ-25-035, March 4, 2025).
alac.application: The cases were raffled to the MCTC of Municipality A and were still at the trial stage, so they had to remain and be heard there. By moving them to City B on his own, Judge Lim exercised a power that belongs only to the Supreme Court. He also inconvenienced the litigants and witnesses, for whose convenience venue exists, and exposed the court records and evidence to risk. His convenience is not a justification.
alac.conclusion: Judge Lim overstepped his authority and is administratively liable for violating Supreme Court rules, directives, and circulars.

notes: Leonen, SAJ. wrote a separate concurring and dissenting opinion (he would have dismissed the respondent); Caguioa, J. concurred; Marquez, J. took no part (prior action as Court Administrator). Only the main opinion is digested. The body cites gross insubordination under "section 14(11)" while the fallo cites "section 14(n)" of Revised Rule 140; this appears to be a text or OCR inconsistency, so the digest refers only to Section 14 (serious charges). The decision applied Revised Rule 140 (A.M. No. 21-08-09-SC), the New Code of Judicial Conduct, and the CPRA as in force at the time. The 2027 syllabus frames judicial ethics under the 2025 Code of Judicial Conduct and Accountability (A.M. No. 25-04-04-SC); this decision does not discuss that Code, so check the corresponding CJCA provisions separately.
